The section also meets all three WSU Composition Program EN1 outcomes (composing processes, genre, audience), and as an international section gives particular emphasis to LO4, treating multilingualism as a rhetorical asset throughout. Unit assignments above are the syllabus’s own “Primary LOs” lines — every item in a unit inherits them, and the same mapping drives the outcomes block in each item’s hover card.

The weekly shape — four sessions
SessionTrackWhat it carries
1ENGL 1010The week’s new concept and reading — input.
2WLC 2040Hear it and say it: the oral work on the same material, placed before the writing it feeds.
3ENGL 1010Write it: application, drafting, workshop.
4WLC 2040Perform, assess, or debrief the speaking.

Two meeting days a week, two sessions on each. Which track sits in which slot is a pedagogical choice, not a fixed timetable — the ordering above follows the course’s own speak first, write second principle from the Rationale Cheat Sheet. Weekdays, clock times, and rooms deliberately appear nowhere in the Canvas pages; the schedule lives in the syllabus. Week 14 (Thanksgiving) has two sessions rather than four, and Week 16 is the finals slot.

Open Canvas-build decisions

Settle these before (or while) building — they change how several weeks get built, so it's cheaper to decide once than to rebuild.

  1. Verify the two rosters are identical — do this first. ENGL 1010 International and WLC 2040 run as one course across two periods, housed in a single Canvas shell so students don't bounce between shells. That only works if enrollment matches exactly. Check with the registrar before relying on it. Any student enrolled in one course but not the other will either be missing required items or seeing items that don't apply to them — and in a combined shell that is invisible until a grade is wrong. If the rosters diverge, the fallback is section-restricted assignments or two shells.
  2. Classic Quizzes vs. New Quizzes. This map assumes New Quizzes for every graded/practice check (grammar-for-writing, vocabulary, source-credibility, reading checks). Confirm WSU Canvas still has Classic Quizzes available as a fallback if a New Quizzes item type (e.g., matching, categorization) doesn't fit a specific check.
  3. Ungraded surveys as Assignments vs. true Quiz-type surveys. The Week 1 intake survey and diagnostic writing sample were built as 0-point Assignments marked complete/incomplete (matching the existing HTML). An ungraded Survey (New Quizzes practice mode, or Classic Quizzes "ungraded survey") would anonymize responses differently — decide per item, especially the intake survey where anonymity isn't wanted (Paul reads these individually).
  4. Built-in Peer Review vs. Discussion-based peer review. Three drafts get workshopped (Literacy Narrative wk 3, Rhetorical Analysis wk 8, Researched Argument wk 13). Canvas's native Assignment → Peer Review auto-assigns reviewers and keeps feedback attached to the submission; a Discussion thread is more visible to the whole class but harder to grade for completion. Recommend native Peer Review for all three.
  5. Module locking. Sequential unlock (can't see Week 3 until Week 2 items are done) vs. everything open from day one. International/multilingual students often value being able to work ahead across time zones — leaning toward open, with only "Prerequisite: previous major draft submitted" locks on the four major assignments.
  6. Assignment Groups & weighting — now carrying two grades, not one. Settled: the ENGL and WLC grades diverge along the writing/speaking line, and Canvas assignment groups are the mechanism. Writing-track items (essays, drafts, written process work, reading quizzes) feed the ENGL 1010 total; speaking-track items (oral language map, listening log, think-pair-share, debate, TED-style presentation) feed the WLC 2040 total. Weight the groups so one shell produces two separable totals, and put every item in its group as it is built — retrofitting group membership across 80+ items is miserable. Within ENGL, keep the scope & sequence split: Major Assessments 75% (15/15/25/10/10), Process Work & Homework 15%, Participation/Peer Review 10%.

    This also resolves the standing scope-and-sequence question about whether speaking earns a formal grade: it does, under WLC. The Unit 2 debate and the Unit 4 TED-style presentation are the two big WLC-graded speaking assessments and should be weighted accordingly.
  7. Rubrics. Five rubrics to build once and reuse: Literacy Narrative, Rhetorical Analysis, Researched Argument, Multimodal Presentation, Reflective Portfolio. Build these before Week 4 so the first one is ready the moment drafts come in.
  8. Library session (Week 10). Needs an actual booking with Stewart Library — once confirmed, add a Page with the session's time/location/librarian contact and link the library's source-evaluation guide.
  9. Campus survey / IRB. Confirm departmental practice on classroom-only survey use before the Week 10 "launch campus survey" Assignment goes live to students.
  10. Conference sign-ups (Week 13). One-on-one drafting conferences need a scheduling mechanism — Canvas Scheduler (Calendar → Appointment Groups) is the natural fit; decide slot length (10–15 min) and publish the sign-up sheet at least a week ahead.

Reconciled against the live Writing Elevated table of contents (11 sections, 28 chapters). WLC 2040 items carry the teal badge and are fully drafted for Weeks 1–15 (32 items). Every page renders at 1200px. 108 items are fully drafted — 76 ENGL 1010 (Weeks 1–13) and 32 WLC 2040 (Weeks 1–15) — each item's HTML is embedded here via its View & copy button, ASCII-clean and ready to paste into Canvas, and renderable in place via Preview. Citations are extracted from the pages themselves, so a hover card is only as good as the page behind it: 94 items carry a 📘 textbook box, 4 cite chapters inline without one, and 10 are instructor-built with no Writing Elevated anchor at all. ENGL Unit 4 (Weeks 14–16) is still a build target; its WLC counterparts are drafted and were written against the planned Unit 4 outline, so give them a light pass once the ENGL pages exist.
